Explore and collect Fabric GraphQL data

Source: vignettes/graphql-schema-and-rows.Rmd
graphql-schema-and-rows.Rmd

Fabric APIs for GraphQL generate their schema from the objects exposed by an API item. fabricQueryR keeps that schema-specific shape explicit: inspect the schema, write a normal GraphQL document, paginate with the connection fields selected by that document, and then identify the exact row path to collect.

Start with a discovered API so its endpoint and workspace travel together:

library(fabricQueryR)

api <- fabric_graphql_apis("Analytics workspace")[[1]]

The caller needs Run Queries and Mutations permission on the API. With SSO connectivity, the caller also needs access to the underlying data source. The package uses the delegated GraphQLApi.Execute.All scope for interactive users and the Fabric audience for service-principal authentication.

Inspect the generated schema

Microsoft Fabric disables runtime introspection by default. Only a workspace admin can enable it under API Settings > Introspection. Once enabled, the standard introspection response is available as a nested R list:

schema <- fabric_graphql_schema(api)

schema$queryType$name
vapply(schema$types, `[[`, character(1), "name")

fabric_graphql_schema() stops with a fabric_graphql_introspection_error when the service does not return a complete schema. Its message points to the administrator setting and the portal’s Export schema alternative. Export remains available when runtime introspection must stay disabled.

Query and paginate rows

Fabric normally represents a generated collection with items, hasNextPage, and endCursor. Request all three pieces needed by the workflow and use a stable explicit ordering when pages must be repeatable:

pages <- fabric_graphql_paginate(
  api,
  query = paste(
    "query Products($first: Int!, $after: String) {",
    "  products(first: $first, after: $after, orderBy: {id: ASC}) {",
    "    items {",
    "      id",
    "      name",
    "      category { id name }",
    "      tags",
    "    }",
    "    hasNextPage",
    "    endCursor",
    "  }",
    "}"
  ),
  variables = list(first = 100L, after = NULL),
  operation_name = "Products",
  next_cursor = fabric_graphql_cursor("products"),
  idempotent = TRUE
)

The cursor is opaque. fabric_graphql_cursor() only reads it from the configured connection path and feeds it back through the after variable; it does not interpret the value.

Build an analysis-ready tibble

Select the row array explicitly relative to each page’s data field:

products <- fabric_graphql_collect(pages, c("products", "items"))

products
attr(products, "complete")
attr(products, "page_count")
attr(products, "errors")

Scalar fields become ordinary columns. A field that first appears on a later page is added to the union of columns, with typed NA values in earlier rows. Nested objects and arrays remain list-columns rather than being flattened:

products$category[[1]]
products$tags[[1]]

JSON whole numbers beyond R’s exact double range are decoded as character values. The collector preserves those strings. If the same field has smaller R integer values on another page, it promotes those smaller values to character too; it never converts the large value to an inexact double. Other incompatible scalar changes stop with an error so a schema change cannot silently alter the analysis.

GraphQL can return data and errors together. The rows remain usable, while the combined service errors stay in attr(products, "errors") and their count is shown when the tibble prints.

Treat incomplete pagination as partial data

fabric_graphql_paginate() marks completion only after the cursor callback reports that no next page exists. Reaching max_pages raises a fabric_graphql_pagination_error whose pages field is marked incomplete. If those pages are passed to fabric_graphql_collect(), collection raises a fabric_graphql_collection_error instead of returning an apparently complete tibble:

tryCatch(
  fabric_graphql_collect(incomplete_pages, c("products", "items")),
  fabric_graphql_collection_error = function(error) {
    partial <- error$partial_data
    attr(partial, "complete")
    partial
  }
)

Fabric currently defaults each page to 100 items and limits pagination to 100,000 items. A response is limited to 64 MB, one request to 100 seconds, and query nesting to 10 levels. Use smaller pages and stable filtered partitions for large results rather than treating a service-limit response as completion.

See Microsoft’s documentation for introspection and schema export, GraphQL limits, and the generated pagination shape.
